meta: Théodore Géricault on his deathbed, painted by his friend Charles Emile Champmartin in 1824 and once taken for Géricault's own work.
about: A dead man lies wrapped in white sheets. For a long time the painting was given to Géricault, until a cleaning uncovered the signature of his friend and follower Charles Emile Champmartin. The museum now says the dead man is Géricault himself, who died of chronic tuberculosis at 32. Images of his death circulated through the 1800s, and copies of his death mask stood in young artists' studios. The museum links his early death and bold art to the idea of the tragic Romantic artist.

meta: Raphaelle Peale's 1822 still life of strawberries, nuts and Chinese porcelain, one of the first American paintings of its kind.
about: Strawberries, nuts and tableware are set out with great care in this still life by Raphaelle Peale, one of the first painters in the United States to specialize in the genre. The museum says he followed 17th-century Dutch still life and added imported goods such as Chinese porcelain made for the American market, a sign of the young nation's growing wealth. The large glass urn may hold strawberries grown out of season in hothouses, which the Peale family tried on their farm outside Philadelphia.

meta: A bat-like creature on a flying cat torments three monks in Goya's Tale-Bearers, plate 48 of Los Caprichos.
about: A bat-like creature rides a flying cat and torments three monks below it. This is plate 48 of Goya's Los Caprichos, 80 etchings published in 1799 that comment darkly on the moral, social and religious faults of late 18th-century Spain. The Spanish word in the title, soplón, can mean a gust of wind or a tattletale. The museum notes that many prints in the series are crowded with monstrous demons.

meta: A priest in huge reading glasses marries a pair of satyrs in Claude Gillot's print of about 1722.
about: A priest in oversized reading glasses presides at a satyr wedding. Claude Gillot mocked marriage in this print from a series on the life of satyrs, and the caption calls the rite a sad feast in which love is buried. The guests are oddly well behaved for creatures known for lust. The museum says the dealer and connoisseur Pierre-Jean Mariette found the imagery of the series especially inventive.
dimensions: Sheet, trimmed within platemark: 25.4 × 33.9 cm (10 × 13 3/8 in.)

meta: Lorraine Reunited with France, a 1737 print by Charles-Nicolas Cochin, who later kept the king's drawing collection.
about: Charles-Nicolas Cochin made this 1737 print, Lorraine Reunited with France. The museum describes him as a very successful engraver who did better than his father and became important in academic life in the middle of the 1700s. In 1752 he was made keeper of the king's drawing collection, and his political position brought him many commissions.

meta: A circus rider prepares to leap through a paper hoop in Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec's Equestrienne at the Cirque Fernando, 1887 to 1888.
about: A circus rider is about to stand up on her galloping horse and jump through a paper hoop held by a clown. The ringmaster Monsieur Loyal cracks his whip, and she seems to snarl at him while he glares back. The museum says Toulouse-Lautrec may have modeled the heavily made-up rider on Suzanne Valadon, a former circus performer and artist he was with for almost three years. The setting is the Montmartre circus that Renoir painted in his portrait of the Wartenberg sisters.

meta: The Annunciation from the wings of Johann Koerbecke's altarpiece for the abbey of Marienfeld, completed by 1457.
about: The Annunciation was one of eight scenes from the life of the Virgin on the inner wings of Johann Koerbecke's altarpiece for the Cistercian abbey of Marienfeld near Münster. On feast days the open wings framed relics and a gilded statue of the Virgin and Child, and their gold backgrounds added to the splendor. The outer sides showed darker Passion scenes in landscapes. The altarpiece was taken apart in the late 17th century, and the panels were scattered in the early 19th.

meta: Friar Pedro ties up the bandit El Maragato in Goya's small painting of about 1806.
about: Friar Pedro de Saldivia ties up the bandit El Maragato after outwitting him. The man had escaped from prison, spent two months stealing, and then tried to take the friar and others hostage. The friar seized his gun, shot him in the thigh as he fled and bound him. That was the end of it. Goya painted a small series about this 1806 event for his own pleasure or for a few patrons. The story was so popular that artists recalled it in pictures, poems and songs.

meta: Two young women brace against the wind on a high overlook at Prout's Neck in Winslow Homer's 1894 watercolor, The Outlook, Maine Coast.
about: Two young women brace themselves against the wind on a high overlook at Prout's Neck, Maine. Homer shows little of what they are looking at. His subject is the act of looking, tied to the feel of strong breezes, damp air and a chilly gray day. The museum says watercolor let him work quickly outdoors and make those effects immediate. The low viewpoint pushes the windy sky of gray and pink clouds to the front.

meta: Hudibras and his squire in the stocks, plate six of William Hogarth's twelve engravings after Samuel Butler's poem, 1725 to 1726.
about: Hudibras and his squire sit in the stocks after losing to the woman Trulla, with his huge boots and weapons piled where the fiddle and case usually sit on the stocks. William Hogarth made twelve engravings of the story from Samuel Butler's mock-heroic poem, which ridicules the hypocrisy of the Presbyterians, Independents and Zealots who hoped to lead the puritan side in the Civil War. This is plate six.

meta: Joseph Ritter von Führich's drawing of about 1830 for Ludwig Tieck's play on Saint Genoveva, based on a medieval legend of betrayed innocence.
about: Joseph Ritter von Führich drew this scene as an illustration for Ludwig Tieck's play on Saint Genoveva, based on a medieval legend of innocence betrayed. In the play her husband wrongly accuses her of unfaithfulness. Führich was a fresco painter active in Rome with the Nazarene Brotherhood, who liked expressive outline and clear detail like Dürer and Raphael. Schumann's only opera, based on the same play, was first performed in Leipzig in 1850.

meta: Saint John the Baptist built from dots and flecks in Giulio Campagnola's stipple engraving of about 1505.
about: Saint John the Baptist stands hard-edged against a bare white ground, built almost entirely from dots and flecks. Giulio Campagnola invented this stipple technique, which became popular for reproductions in the 18th and 19th centuries. He worked in Venice and learned the smoky effects of his teacher Giorgione. The museum says he also used a drawing by Andrea Mantegna to give the prophet his strength.

meta: Heads and paws of lions in studies by Eugène Delacroix, drawn from live caged animals and dissected bodies.
about: Heads and paws of lions fill this sheet of studies. Delacroix never finished academy training, but he kept the habit of drawing from three-dimensional fragments. He sketched details for later paintings from live caged animals and from dissected bodies. The museum notes that his friend Antoine-Louis Barye cast animal parts for his bronzes, while Delacroix's touches of color make these isolated studies livelier.

meta: Eugène Boudin's pastel of the seaside at his home port of Honfleur, about 1860, an influence on the young Monet.
about: Eugène Boudin was born in Honfleur, one of the prettiest harbor towns in Normandy, and this pastel shows its seaside. He taught himself and began trying pastel in the 1850s. The museum thinks a landscape like this was probably made outdoors, and says such work would strongly influence the young Claude Monet.

meta: Schelte Bolswert's engraving of Rubens's Lion Hunt, which Rubens called one of his best paintings in 1621.
about: Schelte Bolswert engraved Rubens's Lion Hunt, and the museum says the print catches the swirling energy of the painting. Rubens cared a great deal about prints made after his work, though he liked the fame they brought. In a letter of 1621 he called the painting nearly finished, entirely by his own hand, and one of his best, with life-size figures. The engraving runs the same way as the painting, which may have been Rubens's own request, since printing normally reverses an image.
dimensions: Image: 40.9 × 58.6 cm (16 1/8 × 23 1/8 in.); Primary support, trimmed within platemark: 42.5 × 59 cm (16 3/4 × 23 1/4 in.); Secondary support: 49.6 × 68 cm (19 9/16 × 26 13/16 in.)

meta: Livio Agresti's design for the altar of Santa Caterina dei Funari in Rome, showing Saint Catherine arguing with philosophers.
about: Saint Catherine argues with philosophers in the upper half of this highly finished drawing, and below she is attended by an angel. The museum explains that it combines two scenes from the Golden Legend. In the first she defends Christianity before Emperor Maxentius and 50 pagan orators. In the second she waits in prison with an angel after the orators were converted. Livio Agresti made it as a design for the high altar of Santa Caterina dei Funari in Rome. Cardinal Federico Cesi ordered the painting, which Agresti began in 1562 or 1563 and Federico Zuccaro finished.

meta: Bartholomeus Breenbergh's large etching Joseph Distributing Grain to Egypt, made in 1644 after he turned to historical subjects.
about: Bartholomeus Breenbergh etched Joseph Distributing Grain to Egypt in large format in 1644. He had lived about ten years in Rome from 1619, and in 1623 he founded a fraternity of Netherlandish artists there. After he returned to Amsterdam and married well, he turned from landscapes to historical and literary subjects, which he showed in big etchings like this one.

meta: Judith stuffs the head of Holofernes into her maid's pouch in Israhel van Meckenem the Young's engraving of about 1495.
about: Judith pushes the head of Holofernes into her maid's pouch while a battle rages in the background. In the biblical story she freed the Hebrews from Assyrian rule by seducing the general and cutting off his head as he lay drunk. Israhel van Meckenem shows it matter-of-factly. The headless body is still visible, but the sword is clean and there is no blood in the scene.
dimensions: Sheet trimmed within platemark: 21.4 × 31.8 cm (8 7/16 × 12 9/16 in.)

meta: Two old Pantaloons in glasses stand before elegant nobles in Jacques Callot's 1616 etching of Commedia dell'arte types.
about: Two old men in glasses and theatrical dress stand in the foreground, both playing the stock Commedia dell'arte figure Pantalone, the grasping old lecher. Jacques Callot filled his lively etchings with clowns, beggars and figures from that improvised street theater. Behind them, elegant nobles dally at ease, in sharp contrast.

meta: Venus and Cupid share a canopied bed in Luca Cambiaso's painting of about 1570, with a quiver set aside.
about: Venus and Cupid share a canopied bed, seen in profile, which gives the scene an unusual intimacy. Doves in the lower left are Venus's emblem, and the dropped quiver with an unbuckled strap shows she has disarmed Cupid, who was known for wounding lovers with his arrows. The museum calls Luca Cambiaso the most important and inventive painter in 16th-century Genoa, with a personal style of simplified, geometric anatomy and dramatic, silvery light.

meta: A murdered woman's ghost returns to haunt her husband in Hokusai's The Mansion of the Plates, from One Hundred Ghost Tales, 1831 to 1832.
about: A woman's ghost haunts the husband who killed her for breaking some plates. He threw her body and the pieces of the dishes into a well, and she came back every night in the eerie form shown here. The print is from Hokusai's One Hundred Ghost Tales of 1831 to 1832, a series he apparently meant to carry to a hundred, though only five prints are known. Its bright blue comes from Prussian blue pigment, which had just become affordable, and the museum says viewers then linked it to death and the occult.

meta: A young Saint John the Baptist with a reed cross and a lamb, recently recognized as the work of Diego Velázquez, about 1622.
about: A young Saint John the Baptist lives as a hermit in the wilderness. His cross of reeds, his pointing hand and the lamb beside him point to his role as the prophet who foretold Christ, the lamb of God. The painting was once given to an unknown Sevillian artist but has recently been recognized as the work of the young Diego Velázquez. The museum thinks it may date from after his short visit to Madrid in 1622, where Italian paintings in the royal collection showed him new ways of painting the figure.

meta: Marie de' Medici, queen mother of Louis XIII, painted by Frans Pourbus the Younger in 1616, six years after naming him her portraitist.
about: Marie de' Medici, queen mother of Louis XIII, sits for Frans Pourbus the Younger six years after she named him her personal portraitist. Pourbus came from a family of portrait painters in the Spanish Netherlands and, like Antonis Mor, served European courts, from Brussels to Paris. The museum says his careful treatment of her elaborate clothes brings out many textures, details and patterns within a limited range of color.

meta: Louis Philippe and Talleyrand as demonic friars in Daumier's 1835 print When the Devil Grew Old, He Became a Hermit.
about: Louis Philippe and his ambassador to Britain, Charles de Talleyrand, appear as demonic friars. Daumier points at the hypocrisy of the regime with a crucified figure of Liberty, a rosary made of coins, Talleyrand's cloven hoof and the king's hooked toenail. The museum notes that Talleyrand's cat looks more tame than devilish, a sign of bourgeois respectability in the middle of the fantasy. The title says that when the devil grew old he became a hermit.

meta: Henri Matisse's Still Life with Geranium of 1906, a still life turned into an Arcadian scene with his own sculptures.
about: Matisse turns a simple still life into a populated Arcadian landscape, in the rapid brushwork and bright, thick color of the Fauves, whom critics saw him leading. The museum points out pairs of contrasts. The upper half is pale and lightly brushed while the lower is darker and heavily painted. A firmly planted female figure faces a male one that almost flees. Red vegetables grown near Paris sit beside ceramics from distant places. The figures are his own sculptures, probably shown as plaster casts, drawn in minimal color and simple lines.

meta: A trained cheetah brings down a black buck in Govardhan's Mughal hunting scene of about 1602 to 1604.
about: A trained cheetah in a red collar brings down a black buck. Mughals used cheetahs like this on hunting trips. The museum reads the scene as a comment on Prince Salim, who loved hunting and wanted to take the throne from his father Akbar. Between 1600 and 1605 Salim set up his own court in defiance of his father. The young Govardhan, a Hindu who would later reach high rank under the next two emperors, was one of the artists who joined him.
credit_line: Dudley P. Allen Fund

meta: A miniature of a woman called Mrs. Close, in pearls and a plum dress, by Horace Hone in 1786.
about: Nobody knows why this sitter is called Mrs. Close. The name has gone with the miniature since at least 1929, when Edward Greene bought it from the dealer Leo Schidlof, but nothing inscribed on it gives her name. Her gown and hair are decorated with strands of pearls against an olive green background, and she wears a plum dress with a lace fichu. She also wears a miniature turned back to front, showing plaited hair on its reverse. The museum says this stresses how private such portraits were. Horace Hone painted her in 1786.
credit_line: The Edward B. Greene Collection

meta: A pond at Ville-d'Avray near Corot's home, painted in the soft, silvery manner of his late years.
about: A pond near Corot's home at Ville-d'Avray, just west of Paris, is painted in his late style of soft, hazy shapes and gentle silvery light. The museum says such pictures join his lifelong study of nature with nostalgic memories, and contrast with the more formal compositions and crisp forms of his early landscapes. His devotion to studying nature directly was a major influence on the Impressionists.
credit_line: Elisabeth Severance Prentiss Collection

meta: A tiger attacks a buffalo in Henri Rousseau's imaginary jungle of 1908, finished after he was let out of prison.
about: A tiger attacks a buffalo in an imaginary jungle where botanical accuracy hardly mattered, and the bananas even grow upside down. Henri Rousseau had never left France and drew on travel books and the Paris botanical garden. He was still working on it in December 1907 while in prison for fraud, and officials let him out early to finish it for the Salon des Indépendants, where it hung in March 1908. The museum calls it one of his largest and most important compositions.
credit_line: Gift of the Hanna Fund

meta: Abraham bows before three angels in a Francesco Guardi painting of the 1750s, one of a series of four.
about: Abraham bows to the ground before three angels in a scene from Genesis 18, set oddly before a marble classical portico where a woman, presumably his wife Sarah, lurks. In the story he met three men at midday and recognized them as angels. Francesco Guardi painted it in the 1750s as one of four pictures in a series. Three of them show episodes from Abraham's life, starting with this one.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: A king picks fruit from the Tree of Life while a loyal parrot watches from its cage, painted by Suraju about 1560.
about: A king picks fruit from the Tree of Life with his own hands and feeds it to a man, while a loyal parrot watches from its cage among the courtiers. The parrot has to prove to the king that the fruit is not poisonous, so that he will not be executed. When the fruit makes an old man young again, the parrot is cleared. Suraju made the painting around 1560.
credit_line: Gift of Mrs. A. Dean Perry

meta: A scholar and his qin-bearing attendant gaze at a waterfall in Tani Bunchō's winter painting of 1790.
about: A scholar and an attendant carrying his qin, a stringed instrument, sit in a mountain pavilion among soaring Chinese mountains. Tani Bunchō painted it in winter and wrote two lines of a poem on it about a stone cliff of layered rocks and waterfalls tumbling from the sky. The museum says viewers in Japan then would think of the poem about a waterfall at Mount Lu by the Chinese poet Li Bai.
credit_line: John L. Severance Fund

meta: A monk reads on the back of a water buffalo in Yamaguchi Sekkei's 1687 painting of Weizheng, with a poem by Nanyuan.
about: A figure reads a text while riding backward on a water buffalo. The painting shows the Chinese monk Weizheng, who lived from 986 to 1049 and was called Zheng of the Yellow Ox after his favorite mount. Yamaguchi Sekkei, a Kyoto painter known for Buddhist subjects, painted it in ink in 1687. The poem about the monk at the top was brushed by Nanyuan Xingpai, a Chinese Buddhist monk who moved to Japan in 1654.
credit_line: Gift of Nisaburo Mizutani

meta: Witches with skulls, brooms and a flayed lizard in daylight in Salvator Rosa's Scenes of Witchcraft: Day, about 1645 to 1649.
about: Hags clutch skulls, wield brooms and slice lizards as they get ready to go to the witches' Sabbath. One of them flays a thrashing lizard for the innards used in magical ointments. Witches usually rode goats, but Rosa gives them an owl, a bird of ill omen. The museum says setting these grotesque women in full daylight adds a comic note and reflects his satirical poetry and his wish to expose human folly. This is the scene of noon, from Rosa's Scenes of Witchcraft.
credit_line: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

meta: A monk looks out of a window with a finger in his book in Ture Nikolaus Cederström's The Sunlight.
about: A monk looks thoughtfully out of a window, holding his place in a book with a finger. Ture Nikolaus Cederström spent much of his career in Munich, where monastic life was a popular subject. The museum says such pictures were liked because they gave a view into private life inside monasteries, which were closed to the public. The monk's relaxed pose and absorption in the view offer an approachable picture of religion and show his longing for the outside world.
credit_line: Gift of the Frances W. Ingalls Trust

meta: General Keith MacAlister in a brown coat and powdered hair, a preparatory sketch by John Smart from about 1800 to 1810.
about: General Keith MacAlister is shown bust-length in three-quarter view, facing right, in a brown coat, white frilled vest and white cravat, with powdered hair. His right eye is clouded and paler than the left, and the museum says the lack of damage or fading shows that this was part of how he looked. A rocky landscape with a small river behind him probably points to a place that mattered to him in Scotland or India. John Smart kept many hundreds of preparatory sketches like this one, and his descendants inherited them.
credit_line: Bequest of Mrs. A. Dean Perry

meta: Captain James West of the Dutton Indiaman in profile, drawn by John Smart in 1785 on the voyage to Madras.
about: Captain James West is drawn in profile facing right, in a blue coat with gold buttonholes, a white waistcoat and a cravat, with powdered hair. John Smart made the finished drawing in 1785, and the museum says it may also have served as a study for an ivory miniature that has not been found. West sailed the Dutton Indiaman from England to Madras several times, including Smart's own voyage in 1785. At least one son of the judge Sir Elijah Impey was on that voyage and had his portrait taken by Smart.
credit_line: Bequest of Mrs. A. Dean Perry

meta: A father finds his child dead after a windy night ride in Odilon Redon's 1866 etching Fear, after Goethe.
about: A father rides through a cold, windy night with his child and finds it dead. Odilon Redon took the subject from Goethe's poem of 1782 and used parallel lines of different density to darken the tone and mood of this etching. The figures and the man's white cape stand out sharply against the scale and tone of the surroundings. Redon made few etchings. He gave this one to his friend, the critic and novelist Joris-Karl Huysmans, and wrote a personal dedication at the bottom.
credit_line: Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland

meta: The Virgin and Child in a heavenly vision in Isaac Oliver's miniature, made about 1605 to 1617 and unique in English art.
about: A tender Virgin and Child float in a heavenly vision. The picture joins the medieval image of the nursing Virgin with the Salvator Mundi. The museum calls it unique in 17th-century England. It draws visually on Rubens and Federico Barocci, whom the well-traveled Isaac Oliver probably knew, and the Virgin and Child are closer to Catholic than to Protestant imagery. Oliver made it between about 1605 and 1617.
credit_line: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund

meta: Maharana Jagat Singh II of Mewar hunts deer dressed as a Bhil in Chokha's painting of about 1735 to 1740.
about: Maharana Jagat Singh II of Mewar hunts deer dressed as a Bhil, in the leaf skirt of that people of western India, with a female tracker. Both wear a belt of bells to scare the animals out of the brush, and she lights them with a lamp held in a pot. The ruler has shot a deer in the neck while a rabbit, antelopes and a boar run off. Chokha painted it around 1735 to 1740.
credit_line: Purchase and partial gift from the Catherine and Ralph Benkaim Collection; Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund

meta: Grapevines circle an eight-panel folding screen in a summer storm, painted by Choe Seok-hwan in the early 1800s.
about: Grapevines sweep in a full circle across an eight-panel folding screen, whipped by the wind of a summer storm, in a painting by Choe Seok-hwan from the early 1800s. The painter used many tones of ink to give the vines a sense of swift movement in the turbulent weather. July is when deep blue grapes ripen and when the monsoon starts in Korea. Grapes had been an artistic motif since they reached Korea around the 7th century, and by the late 19th century they stood for fertility. A big cluster suggests a stable clan with many descendants.
credit_line: Gift from the Collection of George Gund III

meta: Thomas Cole's View of Schroon Mountain after a storm, painted in 1838 in blazing fall color.
about: Thomas Cole painted this view of the Adirondacks in blazing fall colors, although he sketched it in early summer. The museum says the choice likely had nationalist overtones, since Cole once said autumn was the season in which the American forest surpasses all the world. Two years earlier he had written in his Essay on American Scenery that we are still in Eden. He also placed two Indigenous men in the foreground foliage at right. The museum notes that many Native Americans still lived in the Adirondacks, adapting to growing white settlement, logging, mining and tourism.
credit_line: Hinman B. Hurlbut Collection

meta: A bust portrait of the American painter Benjamin West, allegedly by Thomas Lawrence, painted in 1818 or later.
about: A bust-length portrait of the American artist Benjamin West is said to be by Thomas Lawrence, though the attribution is uncertain. Its style recalls other Lawrence portraits of West, including the full-length one in the National Gallery in London. The museum suggests this smaller version may have been painted when West was old and could no longer stand for long. It may also be a copy of the London picture made by Lawrence or one of his pupils.
credit_line: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust

meta: Three regentesses of the Amsterdam leper house at a table with coins and a ledger, painted by Ferdinand Bol in 1668.
about: Three regentesses of the Amsterdam leper house sit at a table with a ledger, an inkwell and coins, which the Rijksmuseum says shows that they kept their own accounts and managed the money. They were probably also in charge of supervising staff and buying goods. From left to right they are Clara Abba, Elisabeth van Duynen and Agatha Munter. The woman on the right rests a foot on a foot warmer. Ferdinand Bol painted the group in 1668.

meta: A family on the terrace of a country house, with four children, a maid and a dog, by Hendrick ten Oever, 1669.
about: A family sits on the terrace of a country house, with four children around the seated parents. A maid holding a dish of fruit also holds the smallest child. The mother hands a peach to the son at left, and the daughter at right holds a peach too. A dog lies at the right. Hendrick ten Oever painted the group in 1669.

meta: Two girls stand arm in arm, one with a pail, in Winslow Homer's 1870 picture at the Cooper Hewitt.
about: Two girls stand together. The one at the left wears a plaid dress and a hat, with an arm around the other's waist and a pail in her right hand, possibly for picking berries. The girl on the right wears a smock dress and a hat and puts an arm over the other's shoulder. Winslow Homer made the picture in 1870. It is in the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum.

meta: A woman holding a lyre in a circular frame with winged angels, a design by Walter Shirlaw from 1880.
about: A bust of a woman holding the head of a lyre sits in a circular frame. Around it runs a narrow oblong border with two outstretched female angels whose wings cross at the top. Below are the head of a putto and wings, and plant and flower motifs fill the background. Walter Shirlaw made it in 1880. It is in the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum.

meta: Four statue designs by Jan Claudius de Cock, among them a masked Cupid, signed in Antwerp in 1726.
about: Four statue designs stand side by side. A youth with a foot on a dog holds a snake and leans on a standing mirror. A girl with a laurel wreath carries a key and a palm branch. A youth wears a winged helmet and carries the caduceus and a lyre. Cupid covers his face with a mask. Captions in Latin and Dutch name wisdom, constancy, eloquence and pretended love. Jan Claudius de Cock signed the sheet in Antwerp in 1726.

meta: A cartouche design of shells, reeds and flowing water with fish, by Pierre-Philippe Choffard, about 1770.
about: A rectangular frame design has a scrolling shell, with a small oval cartouche crowned with reeds above it. Water runs down the sides from the top, and fish, reeds, branches and rockwork form along the lower edges. Below sits a blank rectangular cartouche framed by another shell, with more water pouring from it. Pierre-Philippe Choffard made the print around 1770, and the plate is numbered and lettered.

meta: A man on a throne and a woman with a stringed instrument in François-Thomas Mondon's chinoiserie print La Sultane Favorite, about 1730.
about: A chinoiserie print shows a man seated on a throne with a woman at his right, who holds a stick or pipe and has a stringed instrument in her lap. The throne and the fantastic architecture around them are decorated with rocaille motifs, rosettes, scrolling leaves, fluting and shells. A lidded vase and draped cloth stand to the right. François-Thomas Mondon made the print around 1730. Chinoiserie is the European style inspired by fanciful ideas of China and East Asia.

meta: Ornament designs for locksmiths, with a key handle and eagle heads, plate 5 of Hugues Brisville's Diverses pièces de serruriers.
about: This plate from Hugues Brisville's Diverses pièces de serruriers shows a range of ornaments for locksmiths, made around 1660. At the top is an escutcheon inside an architectural frame, with screws surrounded by fantastic beasts. At the left is the handle of a key. Below is a floral form with eagle heads.

meta: An executioner and a hermit on a stairway in Domenico Mondo's squared drawing of the beheading of Saint Paul, about 1800.
about: Several figures stand on an uneven surface, perhaps a stairway, in this drawing of the beheading of Saint Paul. An executioner in military dress stands at the left with a hand on his hip, and a hermit speaks to him from the right. Sketchy figures, possibly angels, fill the upper half. The sheet is squared with black chalk for enlargement. Domenico Mondo made it around 1800.

meta: The vestibule of the Palais Bourbon with fluted Corinthian pilasters, after a design by Lassurance, a print of about 1710.
about: This print shows one face of the vestibule of the Palais Bourbon, with the door in the center, a niche with a window at right and two windowless niches at left. Fluted Corinthian pilasters decorate the wall, and cartouches decorate the ceiling cove. The inscription gives the design to the architect Lassurance and names Mariette as the publisher. Pierre L'Assurance is the artist listed for the print.

meta: A fireplace wall in the antechamber of the Hôtel de Roquelaure in Paris, designed by the architect Le Roux, about 1710.
about: This print shows a wall in an antechamber of the Hôtel de Roquelaure in Paris, with a fireplace in the middle flanked by double doors. Paintings fill the overdoors and the mantelpiece, and the panels carry acanthus scrolls, shells and flower baskets. The inscription names the architect Le Roux as the designer and Mariette as the publisher. Jean-Baptiste Le Roux is the artist listed.

meta: Kano Mitsunobu's screens of the Tang emperor Ming Huang and Yang Guifei, from the poem Song of Everlasting Sorrow.
about: The story of the Tang emperor Ming Huang and his concubine Yang Guifei unfolds across this pair of screens, based on Bo Juyi's poem Song of Everlasting Sorrow. The tale runs counterclockwise from the lower right of the left screen. At the top of the left screen a party is held as the An Lushan rebellion begins, and Yang Guifei dies in the uprising. At the upper right of the right screen the emperor is alone once it ends. The poem had been known in Japan since the tenth century. Kano Mitsunobu painted the screens around 1590.

meta: A broad beach with colorful boats and chimneys behind it in James McNeill Whistler's Low Tide, painted at St. Ives about 1883.
about: A broad beach fills the foreground and middle ground, and multicolored boats, houses, people and chimneys are packed into the background. Whistler almost certainly painted it at St. Ives in Cornwall in December 1883 or January 1884. It is probably the picture he showed in London in May 1884 as Sands: Blue Note. The museum says he covered the grain of the wooden panel more fully than in Wortley: Note in Green, but at the right he left the gray ground bare to vary tone and texture.

meta: James McNeill Whistler's Note in Blue and Opal: The Sun Cloud, shown among ten St. Ives oils in London in 1884.
about: Whistler's Note in Blue and Opal: The Sun Cloud was one of ten St. Ives oils in his exhibition at the Dowdeswells' Gallery in London in May 1884. An unusually friendly reviewer praised its brilliant color and the high finish of the Cornish landscapes, giving finish a very unconventional meaning. The museum says recent research suggests the review came from one of the gallery owners, with much of it written by Whistler himself.

meta: The Wangchuan Villa, a copy of Wang Wei's garden scroll traditionally attributed to Guo Zhongshu, in the Freer Gallery.
about: This scroll copies the Wangchuan Villa, the garden estate of the poet and painter Wang Wei, who acquired it around 740. Wang wrote twenty quatrains about points of interest in the garden and painted the mood of each, and the result became one of the most revered landscape scrolls in China. Names such as Bamboo Hill, Magnolia Park and White Stone Shallows are written above the scenes. The museum says this is a standard copy of what Wang's original was believed to look like.

meta: Palace women and children light a firecracker for the new year in a painting attributed to Yan Liben, probably a Ming copy.
about: Palace ladies in elegant clothes gather in a courtyard around two small boys, probably princes, who cover their ears as a woman kneels to light a firecracker. Downstairs a serving girl hangs a portrait of Zhong Kui, the Demon Queller, to ward off evil. Blossoming plums and camellias mark the new year. A Ming title slip names the Tang artist Yan Liben, but the museum calls that attribution anachronistic and thinks the painting is probably a mid-Ming copy of a Southern Song work.

meta: Henry Hobson Richardson, architect of Trinity Church in Boston, painted by Hubert von Herkomer in exchange for a house.
about: Henry Hobson Richardson, born in Louisiana and trained in Paris, is best known for Trinity Church in Boston and for a revival style called Richardsonian Romanesque. Hubert von Herkomer wrote during the sittings that Richardson was as solid in friendship as in figure. Richardson paid for the portrait in kind by designing Herkomer's English country house, Lululaund, named for the painter's wife. It was built in 1894 and demolished in 1939, and it was his only building outside the United States.

meta: The actress Minnie Maddern Fiske in a relaxed, thoughtful pose, painted by Maximilien Colin around 1890.
about: Minnie Maddern Fiske, a leading American actress around 1900, appears in a relaxed, introspective pose in Maximilien Colin's portrait. She made her stage debut at three as the young Duke of York in Richard III, and she rose to fame in 1882 in Fogg's Ferry. The museum says she replaced stiff grand-manner acting with a more natural, psychological style, and from the mid-1890s she championed Ibsen. She also fought the Theatrical Syndicate's grip on American theater.

meta: John Charles Frémont, explorer and first Republican presidential candidate, painted by William Smith Jewett in 1861.
about: John Charles Frémont explored routes to the Pacific as an army topographical engineer. He published popular accounts of his western expeditions, often with his wife Jessie Benton Frémont as an uncredited coauthor, and he became California's first senator in 1849. In 1856 he ran for president, the first candidate of the Republican Party. In August 1861 he freed Missouri's enslaved people without authority, and Lincoln removed him from command. William Smith Jewett painted this portrait in 1861.

meta: John Brown in a U.S. Army blanket with manacles half hidden in shadow, painted by Ole Peter Hansen Balling.
about: John Brown is shown fiery, wrapped in a U.S. Army blanket, with manacles on his wrists just visible in the dark shadows at lower right. Ole Peter Hansen Balling based the portrait on an engraving printed in Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper in 1859. Brown had planned the raid of that year on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry to seize arms and start a slave rebellion. It failed, and he was captured, tried and hanged.

meta: Cornelius Vanderbilt, the Commodore, painted by Nathaniel Jocelyn around 1840.
about: Cornelius Vanderbilt, nicknamed the Commodore, started in the rough world of the New York port and had a stake in Hudson River shipping by 1829. He went on to dominate New England steamships and travel to San Francisco, then railroads from New York to western Canada. The museum calls him a ruthless monopolist who beat rivals with rate wars and political pressure. His one big gift was a million dollars to found Vanderbilt University. He died the richest man in the country, and within fifty years his grandchildren had spent the fortune.

meta: Fifteen writers gather at Washington Irving's home in Christian Schussele's imagined group portrait of about 1860.
about: Fifteen famous writers gather at the home of Washington Irving in this imagined scene. The painting came from teamwork. Mathew Brady photographed each writer, including Hawthorne, Longfellow and Emerson, F. O. C. Darley designed the group, and Christian Schussele painted the canvas, while Thomas Oldham Barlow engraved a widely sold print. When it was shown in New York in December 1863, a booklet of 54 pages described it, and its author called it a national picture.

meta: James Armstrong Thome, abolitionist minister, holds Weld's American Slavery as It Is in a portrait by Nathaniel Jocelyn.
about: James Armstrong Thome holds a copy of Theodore Dwight Weld's American Slavery as It Is, a book of eyewitness testimony to which he contributed research. Thome, a Presbyterian minister and abolitionist, was born into a family of enslavers and turned against slavery as a divinity student at Lane Seminary in Cincinnati. In 1836 the American Anti-Slavery Society sent him to the British West Indies to see the effects of emancipation. Nathaniel Jocelyn painted the portrait.

meta: Light in puddles on a dirt road at sunset in Charles Melville Dewey's tonalist painting The Close of Day.
about: Light reflected in puddles picks out the cart tracks in a dirt road that leads to a house with a smoking chimney in the distance, as shadows gather and the sun sets. Charles Melville Dewey was one of the American tonalists, who painted in muted colors and soft-edged, atmospheric effects. The painting is called The Close of Day.

meta: A whale's spout under a cloudy sky in William Morris Hunt's loosely painted The Spouting Whale.
about: A cloudy sky fills most of the picture, and a geyser of water from a whale below the surface is just visible. William Morris Hunt took up landscape in the 1870s and traveled as far as Florida and Mexico for views. The museum says he suggests the whale's power through dark shadows on the choppy water and strong contrasts in the sky. The loose brushwork and indistinct forms give a sense that the whale might surge up at any moment.

meta: A Dutch ship wrecked on a rocky coast while salvagers carry off the cargo, painted by Ludolf Backhuysen about 1700.
about: A ship has run aground on a rocky coast, with the crew hanging from the rigging and bobbing in the surf. On the beach, salvagers are already carrying off casks and bales while the seamen call for help. The museum says it shows the risks of Dutch trade, which brought a golden age to Holland in the seventeenth century and sent ships as far as Southeast Asia. Ludolf Backhuysen learned from two Amsterdam marine painters and became the leading marine painter in Holland.

meta: Mary steadies the child as if helping him take his first step in Peter Paul Rubens's Madonna and Child, a version of an Antwerp altarpiece.
about: Mary gently touches the child's foot with her right hand and steadies him with her left, as if helping him take his first step. The painting is a version of a Madonna in a Rubens triptych ordered around 1617 for Antwerp Cathedral. The museum says the focus is on Christ's humanity more than his divinity. It reached the national collection from John Gellatly, who thought American artists were the equal of any old master and meant his European works as an example for them.

meta: Sarah Goodridge's miniature of her niece Beulah Appleton, made around 1840.
about: Sarah Goodridge painted this miniature of her niece Beulah Appleton, the daughter of her sister Beulah and Thomas Appleton. She also painted another miniature of one of the Appleton children, Sarah, with her cat, Sanko.

meta: Thomas Eakins's pensive portrait of his friend Annie Williams Gandy, called Mother, in a morning coat and braids.
about: Annie Williams Gandy, nicknamed Mother, was a close friend of Thomas Eakins and his wife. He shows her in a morning coat and braids, as if she had just got out of bed, in a quiet, thoughtful moment. Women lost in reverie were a fashionable subject around 1900, but most artists flattered their sitters. Eakins did not hide blemishes and worry lines, and many people found his portraits unflattering. One critic wrote that he could show mere thinking without gesture or pose.

meta: Palm trees, golden sand and a hazy blue sky on Fort George Island, Florida, in a small painting by Thomas Moran.
about: Thomas Moran visited Fort George Island, Florida, with his wife in 1877 and made small studies of its trees and beaches, very different from his sweeping views of Yellowstone. In this picture a hazy blue sky over palm trees and golden sand suggests a romantic desert island where people could escape everyday life. Within twenty years of it, the warm coasts of the Carolinas, Georgia and Florida had become fashionable tourist spots.

meta: Men carry flour sacks from the Hook Windmill in East Hampton under two rainbows in Edward Lamson Henry's painting.
about: Men unhurriedly carry sacks of flour from a windmill to a horse-drawn wagon, and two rainbows in the cloudy sky show that a storm has just passed. The Hook Windmill was the last wind-powered gristmill built in East Hampton, New York. It was built in 1806, worked until 1908 and still stands. Edward Lamson Henry painted it, and critics praised his romantic treatment of farm life.

meta: Adelia Ellender holds berries beside a rosebush with a butterfly in Joshua Johnson's portrait of a Baltimore girl, about 1800.
about: Adelia Ellender lived in Baltimore, where her father was a plasterer. She is dressed like a small adult, as was the custom for children then. The berries in her hand and the butterfly over a rosebush behind her stand for her childhood innocence and for her later change into a lady. Joshua Johnson painted the portrait around 1800.

meta: Keokuk, The Watchful Fox, shows off on his horse for George Catlin, who painted him on horseback after painting him full-length.
about: Keokuk, whom Catlin calls The Watchful Fox and chief of the tribe, asked to be painted on horseback after Catlin had already painted him full-length. Catlin wrote that Keokuk was vain. He rode up and down in front of the canvas at the door of Catlin's quarters at the dragoon post for much of a day while hundreds of soldiers watched. Catlin says the horse was the best on the frontier, that it cost 300 dollars, and that scalps hung from its bridle.

meta: A Choctaw woman with braided hair painted by George Catlin at Fort Gibson in 1834.
about: George Catlin painted this Choctaw woman at Fort Gibson, Arkansas Territory, in 1834. He described her as having her hair in braids and a remarkable expression. The description comes from Catlin's 1848 catalog of his Indian Gallery.

meta: Fort Pierre on the Missouri River, an American Fur Company post in Sioux country, painted by George Catlin.
about: Catlin writes that Fort Pierre was one of the most important and productive posts of the American Fur Company. It stood in the middle of the great Sioux country and took in an enormous number of buffalo robes, which went to New York and other eastern markets. The land around is almost all prairie, with only slight strips of timber along the river and streams. The fort sat on a pleasant plain among grass-covered hills that rose like terraces three or four hundred feet to the prairie.

meta: A Comanche camp on the move with a dog fight on the way, painted by George Catlin.
about: Catlin writes about watching several thousand Comanche on the march, a scene he found laughable. Each horse drags a load, each dog drags a wallet on two poles, if it will, and each wife carries her own, all in a confused mass. He says the dogs start fights that spread to everyone. This painting shows the camp moving, with a dog fight on the way.

meta: Eanger Irving Couse's quick sketch of Walpi Pueblo under cold clouds, painted a year after his first trip to Taos.
about: Eanger Irving Couse painted Walpi Pueblo a year after his first trip to Taos. Like other eastern artists he was struck by the intense light and stark contrasts of northern New Mexico. He painted it as a quick sketch, catching the sudden, lonely chill that comes with clouds at high elevation.

meta: John Cleves Short, an Ohio lawyer and judge, in a miniature by Benjamin Trott from about 1800.
about: John Cleves Short, a lawyer and judge in Ohio, married Elizabeth Bassett Harrison in 1814, a daughter of the ninth president, William Henry Harrison. In this miniature his hair is brushed forward, a fashion that came to America from England. The back holds a ring of hair. Benjamin Trott painted it around 1800.

meta: Anne Hume Shippen, called Nancy, in a rare portrait of a woman by Benjamin Trott, about 1790.
about: Anne Hume Shippen, called Nancy, was admired as sweet to look upon and sweeter to hold. To please her parents she broke off an engagement with the man she loved and married Colonel Henry Beekman Livingston in 1781, which tied the Lees, Washingtons and Livingstons together. She later left him and lived with her parents. Benjamin Trott's portrait is rare because he painted few women early in his career.

meta: A Kansas farmer and two children in a wheat field, John Steuart Curry's study for the war-bond poster Our Good Earth.
about: A noble farmer stands tall in his Kansas wheat field with two carefree children beside him. John Steuart Curry was asked for a monumental war-bond poster in World War II, and he showed how much farming mattered to the war effort. This watercolor is a study for the painting, which was reproduced as a poster captioned Our Good Earth, Keep It Ours.

meta: Claude Monet's Water Lilies of 1906 looks only at the water's surface, from his pond at Giverny.
about: Monet's water garden at Giverny, which he made three years after buying the property in 1890, became his main inspiration for the next two and a half decades. He painted around 250 water lily pictures, moving from views of the pond with its wooden Japanese bridge to monumental, near-abstract works made for his murals at the Orangerie in Paris. This one belongs to a group made between 1903 and 1908. Its nearly square format drops the usual bands of land, sky and water and looks only at the surface, with lily clusters at bottom left and top right.

meta: Thomas Gainsborough's sketchy landscape of meadow, rocks and trees with a dell and weir, about 1782 to 1783.
about: Gainsborough picks out the meadow and the rocks and trees of this broad landscape in a sketchy manner, changing color and brushwork only slightly, and the whole still holds together. Most of his work was portraits, but he insisted that landscape was his first love.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: Robert S. Duncanson's panoramic Vale of Kashmir of 1867, drawn from Thomas Moore's poem Lalla-Rookh.
about: Robert S. Duncanson, based in Cincinnati, was the first African American artist to win recognition at home and abroad. His panoramic Vale of Kashmir is one of his grandest works and draws on an episode in Thomas Moore's poem Lalla-Rookh of 1817, about a Persian princess traveling to India to marry. A courtly party leaves a palace, comes ashore by boat and climbs a monumental stair to a plaza with a fountain. The museum says the landscape still outshines the figures.
credit_line: Sundry Purchase Fund

meta: Jacob van Ruisdael painted this landscape with a windmill in 1646 while still a teenager.
about: Dark forms are piled up in the foreground against a wide, sunlit plain on the left. Jacob van Ruisdael painted this landscape with a windmill in 1646, while still a teenager. The museum says it already shows his way of making the simplest motifs look grand and heroic.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: A dead beech and a low waterfall in Jacob van Ruisdael's wooded landscape of about 1660 to 1670.
about: The silvery trunk of a huge dead tree juts from a dune and leads the eye across a waterfall to a sunlit field far off. Travelers and a dog follow a sandy path there. A ruined building half hidden by trees glows gold in the sun. The museum says dead trees, waterfalls and ruins stood for the passing of time in Ruisdael's landscapes. He gave the cloudy skies equal care, making patterns of light and shadow that reveal the wind.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: A woman in a lace collar and gold jewelry from the studio of Rembrandt, dated 1635 or earlier.
about: A woman's smooth skin is painted in soft, fluid strokes, while thicker strokes pick out her lace collar and gold jewelry, details to please a rich client. The museum says Rembrandt moved from Leiden to Amsterdam at 25 and soon became one of the city's most successful portraitists. Demand was so great that he probably used assistants on this painting, which is catalogued as from his studio.
credit_line: The Elisabeth Severance Prentiss Collection

meta: Tieleman Roosterman, a rich Haarlem cloth merchant, painted by Frans Hals in 1634 at the age of 36.
about: Tieleman Roosterman, a very rich linen and silk merchant in Haarlem, was 36 when Frans Hals painted him. He stands confidently in a sober but costly black suit, with braid and buttons on his sleeves and ribbon rosettes around the waist of his doublet. The broad linen collar and lace-edged cuffs set off the black. The museum says Hals liked strong, visible brushstrokes that convey the energy of his sitters.
credit_line: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund

meta: A man rises from his chair with an unexplained gesture in Lorenzo Lotto's portrait of 1533 to 1534, possibly Girolamo Rosati.
about: An elegantly dressed man seems to rise from his chair, and nobody can say what his gesture means. He might be addressing someone or pointing at something outside the picture. His right hand rests on a paper, and on the table are clover and jasmine, with roses on the trellis, flowers of luck and love. There may once have been a companion portrait of his bride. A recent reading names him Girolamo Rosati, an official in Fermo, with the paper a design for one of his buildings. The museum says the interrupted moment is typical of Lorenzo Lotto.
credit_line: Gift of the Hanna Fund

meta: Isabella Brant, Rubens's first wife, in a warm, lively portrait of about 1620 to 1625.
about: Isabella Brant was Rubens's first wife, and he painted her many times before she died at 35. The museum says this portrait, made at least five years before her death, shows how close the two were through its warm colors, rich brushstrokes and her lively expression.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: Calabazas, jester at the court of Philip IV, shown openly by Diego Velázquez in a full-length portrait of about 1631 to 1632.
about: Calabazas was a jester at the court of Philip IV of Spain, and he had physical and mental disabilities, which Velázquez shows openly instead of hiding. The Spanish court prized and doted on people like him, but Velázquez changed how they were portrayed. The museum says he used the format of a formal full-length court portrait for a person usually seen as marginal, and so gives him a deeply human presence.
credit_line: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund

meta: Jean-Siméon Chardin's still life of herrings on a pantry shelf, about 1735.
about: A humble pantry shelf holds the herrings, which Chardin paints with delicate glazes and roughly dragged thick paint to catch different surfaces and spaces. The museum says he thought deeply about the act of looking, followed new ideas in optics and physics on light, shadow and color, and expected viewers to look closely. He famously worked in private.
credit_line: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund

meta: Turrones, a Venetian glass and walnuts on a stone ledge in Juan van der Hamen's still life of 1622.
about: A wooden box, a dark glass bottle, walnuts, an elaborate Venetian glass and several turrones sit on a plain stone ledge. Turrones are sweets of pine nuts and honey with almonds and hazelnuts. The museum says the picture may not show a real meal, because the artist was playing with contrasts and harmonies of shape, texture and color. Juan van der Hamen worked at the Spanish royal court, and his father came from the Netherlands.
credit_line: John L. Severance Fund

meta: Philippe Rousseau's still life with asparagus of about 1880, in the manner of Chardin.
about: Philippe Rousseau paints food on a simple kitchen table, with rich textures and restrained colors. The museum says he was deeply influenced by Chardin's atmospheric still lifes, which he and other French painters such as François Bonvin rediscovered in the mid-1800s. A comparison with Chardin's work in the same gallery shows it.
credit_line: Bequest of Noah L. Butkin

meta: A bouquet of costly flowers in a glass by Ambrosius Bosschaert, painted in 1606.
about: Ambrosius Bosschaert was one of the first artists to specialize in flower painting, and the museum says he may have been inspired by the botanical gardens and scientific collections of his hometown, Middelburg. The flowers in this bouquet might look ordinary today, but in the 1600s they were costly rarities. Bosschaert painted it in 1606.
credit_line: Gift of Carrie Moss Halle in memory of Salmon Portland Halle

meta: A vase of flowers by Odilon Redon, about 1905, from the late flower still lifes that brought him his greatest commercial success.
about: Flower still lifes like this filled the last fifteen years or so of Odilon Redon's career and brought him his best sales. His interest began in youth. The child of wine producers, he grew up northwest of Bordeaux and learned how weather and light affect the grape harvest. At 20 he met Armond Clavaud, a botanist and draftsman who illustrated the flowers of the Bordeaux region, and Clavaud's careful drawings helped give Redon his wish to paint nature as seen in a dream.
credit_line: Gift of Roberta Holden Bole

meta: Peonies, hydrangeas and lilacs spill from a dark background in Claude Monet's Spring Flowers of 1864.
about: Peonies, potted hydrangeas and a basket of lilacs spill downward and outward from the geraniums at the back, set against a dark background. The museum says this early still life shows Monet's interest in fleeting effects, which later became his main subject. It is painted with almost scientific accuracy, yet it feels fresh and immediate. Monet's energetic brushwork conveys the play of light on leaves and petals. He painted it in 1864.
credit_line: Gift of the Hanna Fund

meta: Emanuel de Witte's imagined church interior with features of the Oude Kerk in Amsterdam, painted about 1680.
about: This spacious church interior is largely imaginary, but De Witte's precise architecture convinces us that it is a real place. To make it feel familiar he included some features of the Oude Kerk in Amsterdam. In the late 1500s militant Protestants took over Catholic churches in the Netherlands and stripped them of rich decoration and images they called idolatrous. The bare whitewashed interiors that resulted became a favorite subject for Dutch artists, who were drawn to the play of light and shadow on plain walls and to the challenge of showing deep space.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: A quiet interior with a table, teapot and cups by Gwen John, 1915, one of four versions of the subject.
about: Gwen John worked slowly and carefully and produced fewer than 200 paintings in her life. This quiet interior with a table, teapot and cups is small, muted in color and restrained in mood, like all her work. She wrote to a friend that she might never have anything to express except this desire for a more interior life. It is one of four paintings of the same subject, and the others are in the National Museum of Wales, the Yale Center for British Art and the Yale University Art Gallery.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: Tourists, churchgoers, nobles and artists under the dome of the Pantheon in Giovanni Paolo Panini's view of Rome, 1747.
about: Foreign tourists, local churchgoers, Roman nobles and artists mingle under the dome of the Pantheon. Panini shows how many roles this public space had. The building began as a temple under the emperor Hadrian around AD 125 and became a Christian church in 609, and it was restored in the early 1700s. Through the door the portico is visible, where the city's most important art fair was held.
credit_line: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

meta: A woman winds yarn from the hands of a suitor in Eastman Johnson's Nantucket kitchen scene of 1872.
about: A woman winds a ball of yarn from a coil held in the hands of a man who sits across from her at a polite distance, in a rustic kitchen on Nantucket. Winding yarn was a common sign of courtship then, with a joke about a woman ensnaring her suitor. The second woman is probably a chaperone. The museum says the suitor's coarse, open-legged pose and his rude habit of putting his hat on the floor add to the comedy for audiences of the time.
credit_line: Hinman B. Hurlbut Collection

meta: Road menders under huge plane trees in autumn, painted by Vincent van Gogh at Saint-Rémy in 1889.
about: Van Gogh painted this autumn landscape while living in a psychiatric hospital near Saint-Rémy, where he was treated for severe depression. His doctor let him paint landscapes outdoors, since working from nature eased his symptoms. In a letter to his brother Theo he described the scene: workers repairing the pavements under enormous plane trees, with heaps of sand and stones, yellowing leaves, and a house front here and there. The museum shows it near his Two Poplars from the same year.
credit_line: Gift of the Hanna Fund

meta: Two poplars twist against a darkening sky in Vincent van Gogh's autumn landscape painted at Saint-Rémy in 1889.
about: Van Gogh painted this autumn landscape while he was in a psychiatric hospital near Saint-Rémy in southern France. At first he was limited to painting in his room, but he soon went back to working outdoors. Trees twist and lean against a darkening sky, and the intense colors laid on with charged brushstrokes convey his emotional response. The museum says the painting shows the full power of his mature style.
credit_line: Bequest of Leonard C. Hanna Jr.

meta: The Doge's Palace in Venice, painted from a boat by Richard Parkes Bonington in 1826.
about: Bonington became famous overnight at the Paris Salon at 22, and two years later, in 1826, he went to Venice. At first constant rain depressed him. Then the weather changed and the city was at its best. He often painted outdoors to catch quick impressions of the architecture and sunlight. He made this study from a boat anchored in the lagoon near the Doge's Palace. The museum says the thick swirls of paint, mixed while still wet, show how fast he worked.
credit_line: John L. Severance Fund

meta: A cupid tugs Pan toward Venus in Nicolas Poussin's witty Nymphs and a Satyr, about 1625 to 1627.
about: A playful cupid tugs Pan, the goat-legged god of the woods, toward Venus, the goddess of love. The painting illustrates the Latin phrase amor vincit omnia, love conquers all, with a pun on the Greek pan, which means all. Poussin, like Claude Lorrain, set historical and mythological subjects in landscapes inspired by the country around Rome, and his themes often held witty allusions to classical texts. The woodland setting stands for the paradise of Pan's home.
credit_line: Gift of J. H. Wade

meta: A river or canal on the outskirts of Paris by Henri Rousseau, painted between about 1897 and 1905.
about: Besides his large jungle scenes, Rousseau painted small landscapes like this view of a river or canal on the edge of Paris. He keeps sharp, detailed objects but gives up the flat tone of his early work for more blended modeling and freer brushwork. The clouds, trees and houses each take their own place in space. Rousseau was self-taught and quit his job in the Paris toll service at 41 to devote himself to art.
credit_line: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

meta: An unidentified woman in Amedeo Modigliani's elongated portrait of about 1917 to 1918.
about: Amedeo Modigliani was born into a Sephardic Jewish family in Livorno, studied briefly in Florence and Venice, and moved to Paris in 1906. His portraits, known for subtle color and elegantly elongated forms, recorded the lives of fellow artists and poets. The woman in this painting has never been identified.
credit_line: Gift of the Hanna Fund

meta: A bird sleeps head down on a plum branch in Yang Ki-hun's Korean painting of the early 1900s.
about: A bird sleeps on a plum tree. The plum stands for the pure spirit of scholars, an idea that goes back to Lin Bu's poem about tiny plum flowers, and it was also painted in Korea as one of the Four Gentlemen. Here the plum and the bamboo express that scholarly spirit. The museum reads the bird's downward-pointing head as the artist's feeling about the unstable end of the Joseon period. Yang Ki-hun was a scholar-official famed for painting and calligraphy, and King Gojong was one of his patrons.
credit_line: John L. Severance Fund

meta: Death rides a pale horse past a horse race in Albert Pinkham Ryder's The Race Track, begun in the 1890s.
about: Ryder took his subject from a horse race in New York in 1888, after which a friend who had bet 500 dollars on the loser killed himself. Medieval symbolism fills the picture. Death rides a horse as a skeleton with a scythe to cut down the living, and a snake, a sign of temptation and evil, slithers in the foreground. Ryder was an intense man who worked on the painting for several years and hated to part with it.
credit_line: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

meta: Caravaggio's Crucifixion of Saint Andrew, painted in 1606 to 1607, shows the saint's martyrdom as a private, intimate event.
about: Saint Andrew tried to bring Christianity to Greece in the first century and was sentenced to die on the cross for refusing to honor pagan gods. For two days he preached from the cross to a crowd that grew more sympathetic. When his would-be executioners tried to untie him at the crowd's demand, their hands were mysteriously paralyzed, and he died in divine light. The museum says Caravaggio draws the viewer closer by making the crucifixion intimate and private instead of a gruesome public show. Bold contrasts of light and dark suggest the presence of God.
credit_line: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund

meta: A late afternoon view of Boston Harbor with a steamboat at left, painted by Fitz Henry Lane about 1846 to 1847.
about: This is a late afternoon view of Boston Harbor, and the museum says Lane evokes the diffuse light of sunlight on water. He was the son of a shipbuilder, and his ships and their rigging are painstakingly accurate. At the far left a steamboat, a sign of new technology, carries passengers between Boston and Gloucester.
credit_line: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund and partial gift of Travers Newton, Joanna Newton Riccardi and Georgia Newton Pulos

meta: Camille Monet in the snow passing the French doors of their home at Argenteuil, in Claude Monet's The Red Kerchief.
about: This painting shows Monet's first wife, Camille, outside on a snowy day, passing the French doors of their home at Argenteuil. Her face is made of nothing more than quick daubs of paint, a radically bold Impressionist technique. The snow and trees are defined by broad, broken strokes of pure white and green.
credit_line: Bequest of Leonard C. Hanna Jr.

meta: The rulers of Saxony hunt a stag near Hartenfels Castle in Lucas Cranach's painting of 1540.
about: The Protestant rulers of Saxony ordered this lively hunting scene, set near their residence, Hartenfels Castle, seen in the background. John Frederick the Magnanimous stands at the bottom left in dark green hunting dress, spanning his crossbow and waiting for his courtiers and dogs to drive a stag across the river. His wife, the Electress Sibylle, stands at right, ready to take the first ceremonial shot. Hunts with dogs were elaborate, rehearsed occasions guided by hunting horn signals. Cranach dated the picture 1540 and signed it with a winged snake at lower right.
credit_line: John L. Severance Fund

meta: A nude woman throws herself into the sea in Paul Gauguin's In the Waves, painted at Pont-Aven in 1889.
about: A nude figure throws herself into the sea in this picture painted at Pont-Aven in northwest France. The museum reads it as a metaphor for a modern European woman giving up civilization for her natural, primitive instincts. The simplified lines and exaggerated colors, above all the contrast of green and orange, look invented rather than seen. Gauguin showed it at the Café Volpini in Paris in 1889 and so made himself a leader of the Symbolist movement.
credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. William Powell Jones

meta: Monet's monumental Water Lilies, painted between about 1915 and 1926 at Giverny, leaves out the horizon and banks.
about: Claude Monet was a skilled gardener as well as a painter, and he spent the last 30 years of his life painting the private garden he designed at Giverny. This huge view of his water lily pond focuses on the momentary effects of sunlight as it passes through and reflects off the shimmering surface. By leaving out the horizon and the banks, Monet suggests a limitless expanse. The very wide horizontal format fills the viewer's field of vision and adds to that effect.
credit_line: John L. Severance Fund and an anonymous gift

meta: A dark ruined villa and wind-tossed cypresses by the sea in Arnold Böcklin's Ruin by the Sea, 1881.
about: A dark, ruined villa is made stranger by cypress trees tossed by the wind, and a nervous green light flickers over the scene. Böcklin was influenced by German Romantic art of the early 1800s and preoccupied with dreamlike images that suggest death.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: Winslow Homer's Early Morning After a Storm at Sea, painted at Prouts Neck in 1900 to 1903 over four sessions.
about: The Atlantic surf pounding the empty coast at Prouts Neck, Maine, gave Homer the main subject of his dramatic late paintings. He called this one the best picture of the sea he had painted. He first planned it as a watercolor, then did it in oil after nearly twenty years away from the medium. He waited patiently for the right weather and worked on it in four sessions over two years.
credit_line: Gift of J. H. Wade

meta: Saint Jerome beats his chest with a stone before a skull in Jusepe de Ribera's painting of about 1638 to 1640.
about: Saint Jerome translated biblical texts into Latin and sometimes appears as a scholar in his study. Ribera shows him as a penitent who withdrew to the desert, beating his chest with a stone to share Christ's suffering and looking at a skull that stands for human vanity. Ribera worked in Naples and eagerly took over Caravaggio's strong light and dark and his use of naturalistic models.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: The Piazza San Marco in Venice seen by Bernardo Bellotto, nephew of Canaletto, about 1740.
about: This view of the Piazza San Marco shows Bellotto's faithful observation. On the left are the church of San Marco and the Doge's Palace beyond it, leading to the lagoon. The campanile divides the canvas, with the Procuratie Nuove stretching to the right. At the far right stands the church of San Geminiano, which Napoleon removed in the 19th century. Bellotto was Canaletto's nephew and student, and like his uncle he made views of Italy, especially Venice, which British aristocrats on their travels bought eagerly.
credit_line: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund

meta: A Chinese porcelain bowl as valuable as the gold object beside it in Cornelis de Heem's still life with crayfish and oysters.
about: The porcelain bowl in this still life most likely came from China. Political turbulence there had cut off ceramic exports to the West by the 1640s, so the museum says the bowl would have been seen as at least as valuable as the gold object on the table.
credit_line: Bequest of Muriel Butkin

meta: François Boucher's Fountain of Venus of 1756, where some figures are painted gray like stone and others are living.
about: Light, erotic decoration stayed popular with the French aristocracy through the 1700s. Part of the fun here comes from Boucher painting some of the figures in gray, as if carved in stone, and the others fully alive. He plays with the line between painting and sculpture and between fiction and reality. The original purpose of the painting is unclear. It may have been shown as an independent work, but it probably began as a preliminary design for a woven wall hanging.
credit_line: The Thomas L. Fawick Memorial Collection

meta: Dunes and a summer light at Shinnecock in William Merritt Chase's The Old Road to the Sea, about 1893.
about: William Merritt Chase, one of the most influential American Impressionists, ran his own summer school at Shinnecock on the eastern tip of Long Island. He and his students were among the first American artists to paint outdoors, drawn to the low dunes and beaches. The museum says varied brushwork and warm colors make this one of his best Shinnecock pictures, and the panorama glows with summer light. The school ran from 1891 to 1902 and spread Impressionism in the United States.
credit_line: Gift of Mrs. Henry White Cannon

meta: A woman gazes at a bust of Kaiser Franz Josef on Adolf Karpellus's 1916 poster for the exhibition Our Emperor.
about: A woman gazes lovingly at a bust of Kaiser Franz Josef and holds garlands of roses. The poster announces an exhibition of 80 original paintings of episodes in the Kaiser's life, with all proceeds going to the widows and orphans of the armed forces and to the Red Cross. It gives the place, hours and entrance fee. Adolf Karpellus made it in 1916.

meta: Two women and a table of preserves on an anonymous Canadian poster of 1914, Waste not, want not, urging people to prepare for winter.
about: A young woman and an older woman stand before a table of fruit, vegetables and canned goods, and the older woman holds up a jar and gestures at the table. The text on the poster says to save perishable foods by preserving them now. It is an anonymous Canadian poster, catalogued as 1914, titled Waste not, want not, prepare for winter.

meta: A couple with hoarded flour and sugar watch a policeman pass in a Canadian food poster asking Are you breaking the law?
about: A man and woman with bags of hoarded flour and sugar look at the silhouette of a policeman passing their blind-covered window. A statement of the Canada Food Board hangs on the wall, listing the fines for hoarding. This anonymous Canadian poster asks whether you are breaking the law and says patriotic Canadians will not hoard food.

meta: A Dutchman, an Englishman and an American share a table in Utagawa Hiroshige II's Japanese print of 1860.
about: Three men gather around a table. A Dutchman in a tricorn hat holds a pipe, an Englishman drinks from a glass, and an American in a feather headdress holds a telescope. Utagawa Hiroshige II made this Japanese print in 1860, and the Library of Congress holds it.

meta: A soldier cuts the bonds of a Jewish man on an anonymous Canadian poster of 1914 with portraits of three British politicians.
about: A soldier cuts the bonds from a Jewish man, who strains toward soldiers running in the distance and says that now he is free he wants to help set others free. Portraits above show three Jewish members of the British parliament, Herbert Samuel, Viscount Reading and Edwin Montagu. It is an anonymous Canadian poster, catalogued as 1914, and the Library of Congress holds it.

meta: A train, a rickshaw, a bicycle and other vehicles crowd an anonymous Japanese print of about 1870, Melange of vehicles.
about: Various forms of transport crowd this Japanese print. They include a train, a horse-drawn carriage, a horse-drawn trolley, a rickshaw, a bicycle and hand-drawn carts. A man draws water from a well, and a woman walks with a child on her back. The artist is anonymous, and the Library of Congress catalog dates the print to 1870.

meta: A woman with a violin looks at a soldier with a rifle in Utagawa Yoshikazu's Sights in Yokohama, 1860.
about: A woman holding a violin sits in a room in a foreign settlement house and looks at a soldier with a rifle who stands at the right, possibly her husband. He is shown outside the room, perhaps as a figment of her imagination. Utagawa Yoshikazu made this Japanese print in 1860.

meta: A Canadian soldier holds a drowned Red Cross worker and shakes his fist at a German submarine on a 1918 Victory Bonds poster.
about: A Canadian soldier holds a drowned Red Cross worker and raises his fist at sailors on a nearby German submarine. The poster alludes to the sinking of the Canadian Red Cross ship Llandovery Castle, and its title says that Victory Bonds will help stop this. It is an anonymous Canadian poster, catalogued as 1918.

meta: An American ship at Yokohama loaded by small boats and a gangplank, in Utagawa Sadahide's five-sheet print of 1861.
about: An American ship lies in the harbor at Yokohama, with small boats ferrying cargo that is carried up a gangplank onto the busy main deck. Utagawa Sadahide made this five-sheet print in 1861, and the Library of Congress holds it.

meta: An archer shoots at a target down the long hall of Sanjūsangendō in Kyoto in Utagawa Toyoharu's print of 1764.
about: In this view of Sanjūsangendō, a Buddhist temple that holds 1001 statues of the goddess Kannon, an archer kneels at one end of the long wooden hall and shoots at a target at the other. The judge's stand is shown, along with a long promenade on the left with many pedestrians and street vendors. Utagawa Toyoharu made the print in 1764.

meta: A man in a lounge chair imagines himself at war in a 1915 Canadian poster asking Why don't I go? The 148th Battalion needs me.
about: A man relaxes in a lounge chair with a newspaper open to the sports pages and sees himself in combat in the smoke from his pipe. The soldier in combat sees a hockey game in the smoke of a bomb. Small scenes below show dining, dancing, theater, skating, hockey and baseball. The poster, catalogued as 1915, asks why he doesn't go, since the 148th Battalion needs him.

meta: A smoking artillery piece above a river on a 1915 German poster for an artillery display in Karlsruhe.
about: A smoking artillery piece sits between barrels overlooking a river. The poster announces a public display of artillery pieces on the Rennbuckel in Karlsruhe to raise money for Regiment 50 of the 1st Artillery Division, and it gives directions to the exhibit. It is an anonymous German poster of 1915.

meta: A fist smashes a German border marker on a Bavarian People's Party election poster of 1920.
about: A huge fist smashes down on a German border marker, with skulls and a church being blown up on one side and the towers of Munich's Frauenkirche and mountains on the other. The text is a poem saying that the enemy, which it names as Communism, is in Bavaria. It urges people to resist by supporting the Bavarian People's Party. The poster is anonymous and catalogued as 1920.

meta: A sword in a mound of earth, a plowman and a sower: J. V. Cissarz's 1916 poster for the Württemberg War Exhibition in Stuttgart.
about: A sword with an eagle on the hilt is plunged into a mound of earth. Below it a man plows and a woman sows seeds, and smoke and flames from factories rise behind. The poster announces a war exhibition in Stuttgart from May to September, organized by the Württemberg Red Cross under the patronage of the King and Queen and the War Ministry. J. V. Cissarz made it in 1916.

meta: A haloed figure on a pillar welcomes soldiers home in Walter Ditz's 1915 poster, Heroes from the front.
about: A holy figure with raised arms and a white halo stands on a pillar in a robe marked with a cross, with flowers at its foot. The text welcomes home the heroes of the front, saying their homeland greets them and they are heartily welcome. Walter Ditz made the poster in 1915.

meta: A German soldier with grenades in both hands in Hans Rudi Erdt's 1918 poster for a film, Hellish Battle on the Aisne.
about: A German soldier in battle is seen from the side, with his rifle slung over his shoulder, grenades in both hands and a bag of grenades at his shoulder. Flames surround him. The text is the title of a film about the battle on the Aisne. Hans Rudi Erdt made the poster in 1918.

meta: A man with a long box looks back through clouds at travelers above the sea in Utagawa Kunisada's View of Yui, 1837.
about: A man with a long box over his shoulder looks back through clouds from a mountain pass at Yui station on the Tōkaidō Road. He looks toward travelers standing on a cliff above the sea, with sailboats and Mount Fuji beyond. Utagawa Kunisada made the print in 1837.

meta: A celestial dancer stands on a man to reach her feather mantle in Ishikawa Toyonobu's 1764 print of Hagoromo.
about: A woman, possibly a celestial dancer, stands on a man to take down her feather mantle, which hangs on the branches of a tree. The man is helping her get the mantle back in exchange for the chance to see her celestial dance. Ishikawa Toyonobu made this updated version of Hagoromo in 1764.

meta: A blind soldier led by a wounded comrade on a 1917 German poster for a Christmas exhibition for war invalids in Munich.
about: A blind soldier is led by a soldier with his arm in a sling. The poster announces a Christmas exhibition for war invalids, especially the blind, sponsored by the Social Association of Munich Artists, with the place and times given. It is an anonymous German poster of 1917.

meta: Taira no Kiyomori holds a fan toward the sun over the sea in Tsukioka Yoshitoshi's print of about 1880.
about: Taira no Kiyomori stands full-length and faces left, holding a fan in his raised right hand and looking across the sea at a rising or setting sun. A young woman stands at the right. Tsukioka Yoshitoshi made the print around 1880, and the Library of Congress holds it.
